skills.name: Name the strands of Pre-Technical Studies and say how it is used in daily life
skills.mastery: The child names the five strands (foundations and safety, communication and drawing, materials, tools and production, entrepreneurship), puts an activity in the right strand, and says the learning area is used in homes, workshops, farms, shops and offices by everybody. The child does not say it is only for boys, only for people who will become mechanics, or only done in a school workshop. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say which strand a described activity belongs to
say how Pre-Technical Studies helps in a described daily-life job
say who uses Pre-Technical knowledge: girls, boys, workers, businesses
find the false step in a learner's reason

misconceptions.error: Thinks Pre-Technical Studies is only about handling tools and making things.

example.question: Which of these is part of Pre-Technical Studies?
example.wrong_answer: Only using tools in the workshop
example.correct_answer: Tools, drawing, materials, computers, safety and starting a business

misconceptions.cause: The child saw only the workshop lessons.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only using tools in the workshop" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List the five strands and one activity from each.
misconceptions.feedback: Pre-Technical Studies also covers safety, drawing, materials, computers and entrepreneurship, not only tools.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks Pre-Technical Studies is for boys or for learners who will not go on to other careers.

example.question: Who uses Pre-Technical knowledge?
example.wrong_answer: Only boys who will become mechanics
example.correct_answer: Girls and boys, in many jobs and in daily life

misconceptions.cause: Workshop work is pictured as a boys' job.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only boys who will become mechanics" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Name a woman who uses it: a tailor, an engineer, a salon owner, a farmer with a pump.
misconceptions.feedback: Everybody uses it: girls and boys, in homes, shops, farms, offices and workshops.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks Pre-Technical knowledge is used only in a school workshop.

example.question: Where is Pre-Technical knowledge used in daily life?
example.correct_answer: At home, in shops, on farms and in workshops

misconceptions.cause: The child links the subject to a room, not to daily life.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only in the school workshop" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List what happens at home: cooking safely, mending a chair, a phone, a budget.
misconceptions.feedback: Safety, tools, drawings and small businesses are part of daily life everywhere.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

discuss safety rules and regulations to observe (when performing tasks, handing materials and tools),

How can online threats be safeguarded against?

skills.name: Identify safety threats: falls, slips, trips, road crashes, fires and threats to devices
skills.mastery: The child names a fall (from a height), a slip (on a wet or smooth floor), a trip (over an object in the way), a road crash and a fire from sparks, flames, faulty wires or cooking, and names theft, floods or fire, and hardware failure as threats to a device. The child does not call all of them "accidents that cannot be prevented". Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the threat in a described situation
say what could go wrong with a device
pick the situation that is a slip or a trip
find the false step in a learner's reason

skills.name: Identify online threats and say what to do about them
skills.mastery: The child names cyberbullying (hurting someone online), impersonation (pretending to be someone else), phishing (a fake message that tricks you into giving a password or PIN), hacking (breaking into an account or device) and an unknown friend request, and says: do not share a PIN or password, do not open unknown links, do not accept strangers, and tell a trusted adult. The child does not say a message is safe because it looks official. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the online threat in a described message
say what to do with a request from a stranger
pick the safe action
find the false step in a learner's reason

skills.name: Give the safety rules for working with materials and tools
skills.mastery: The child says: wear the right protective clothing (overall, closed shoes, gloves, goggles), tie back long hair and do not wear loose clothes near machines, keep the floor and the bench clean and dry, use a tool only for its job, never run or play in the workshop, switch off and unplug a machine before changing anything, report every injury or accident to the teacher, and know where the fire sand, extinguisher and first aid box are. Power, heat and sharp tools are used with a teacher. The child does not say a small cut need not be reported. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the rule that prevents a described accident
say what a worker should do in a described situation
decide who broke a rule in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

misconceptions.error: Treats a slip and a trip as the same thing.

example.question: Kamau steps on a wet floor and his feet slide away. What is this?

misconceptions.cause: Both words are used loosely.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A trip" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A slip is sliding on a smooth or wet surface; a trip is catching the foot on something.
misconceptions.feedback: A slip happens on a wet or smooth floor. A trip happens when the foot catches on something in the way.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks fires start only from big flames, not from wires, chargers or cooking oil.

example.question: Which can start a fire?
example.correct_answer: A faulty wire, an overloaded socket or hot cooking oil

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures fire as a bonfire.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only a big open flame" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List five ways a fire can start in a house or a workshop.
misconceptions.feedback: Faulty wires, overloaded sockets, hot oil and sparks can all start a fire, not only a big flame.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the only threat to a phone or computer is a thief.

example.question: Which can harm a computer?
example.correct_answer: A thief, a flood or fire, or a hardware fault

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks only of theft.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only a thief" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what happens to a computer in a flood, in lightning or when the power surges.
misconceptions.feedback: Theft, floods, fire and hardware failure can all harm a device.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks road crashes only harm drivers on highways.

example.question: Who is at risk from road crashes?
example.correct_answer: Pedestrians, cyclists, boda boda riders, passengers and drivers

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures a highway crash.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only drivers on highways" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List who is on a road outside the school gate.
misconceptions.feedback: Walkers, riders and passengers are at risk too, near the school gate as well as on highways.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a message is safe if it looks like it comes from a bank or M-Pesa.

example.question: A message that looks like M-Pesa asks you to send your PIN. What is it?
example.wrong_answer: A real message, because it looks official
example.correct_answer: Phishing, a trick to get your PIN

misconceptions.cause: Logos and good spelling feel trustworthy.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A real message, because it looks official" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show that anybody can copy a logo. Real companies never ask for a PIN.
misconceptions.feedback: Phishing messages copy real logos. Nobody real asks for your PIN or password.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks it is fine to accept a friend request from someone met only online.

example.question: A stranger sends you a friend request. What should you do?
example.wrong_answer: Accept, because more friends is better
example.correct_answer: Not accept, and tell a trusted adult

misconceptions.cause: The child links friends with popularity.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Accept, because more friends is better" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: would you give a stranger at the gate your home address?
misconceptions.feedback: Do not accept a stranger. Tell a trusted adult about the request.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks cyberbullying is only a joke because nobody is hit.

example.question: Is hurting someone with nasty messages harmful?
example.wrong_answer: No, words online do not hurt
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is cyberbullying and it hurts

misconceptions.cause: The harm is not seen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, words online do not hurt" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask how a nasty message to you would feel; a message can be kept and shared.
misconceptions.feedback: Cyberbullying hurts like bullying in person. Tell a trusted adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks impersonation means using a nickname.

example.question: Someone makes an account with your friend's name and photo. What is this?

misconceptions.cause: The two ideas both involve a changed name.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A nickname" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A nickname is open and harmless; impersonation pretends to be a real person to trick others.
misconceptions.feedback: Impersonation is pretending to be another real person, usually to trick people.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks hacking happens only to banks and never to a child's phone or account.

example.question: Who can be hacked?
example.correct_answer: Anyone with a weak password or a careless click

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks only of big news stories.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only banks and big companies" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what a thief would want from a child's social media account.
misconceptions.feedback: Anyone can be hacked. Strong passwords and careful clicking protect you.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks working fast is safer or better in a workshop.

example.question: Which habit keeps you safe in the workshop?
example.correct_answer: Work carefully and follow the steps

misconceptions.cause: Speed feels like skill.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Work as quickly as possible" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what happens to a hand that hurries near a saw.
misconceptions.feedback: Rushing causes accidents. Work carefully and follow the steps.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a small cut or a near miss need not be reported.

example.question: You cut your finger a little. What should you do?
example.correct_answer: Tell the teacher and clean the cut

misconceptions.cause: The child fears trouble or thinks it is small.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Say nothing, it is small" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A cut can be dirty; the teacher can also fix what caused it.
misconceptions.feedback: Always tell the teacher about an injury, however small.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks long hair or loose clothes do no harm near a machine.

example.question: What should you do with long hair in the workshop?

misconceptions.cause: The hazard is not obvious.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Leave it loose" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show how a loose sleeve could be caught by a moving part.
misconceptions.feedback: Hair and loose clothes can be caught by moving parts. Tie hair back.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks tools can be left anywhere on the floor or bench.

example.question: Where do tools go when the job is done?
example.wrong_answer: Anywhere, on the floor is fine

misconceptions.cause: The child does not see the trip risk.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Anywhere, on the floor is fine" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask who might step on a tool left in a walkway.
misconceptions.feedback: Tools left about cause trips and cuts. Put them back in their place.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Explain data and information and the characteristics of a computer
skills.mastery: The child says data is raw facts and figures, information is data that has been processed so that it means something, and names speed, accuracy, versatility, reliability, diligence (it does not get tired), storage and consistency, with an example of each. The child says a computer follows instructions and gives wrong output from wrong input. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say whether an item is data or information
pick the characteristic described
say what a computer will do with wrong input
find the false step in a learner's reason

skills.name: Classify computers by function, purpose and size
skills.mastery: The child says analogue computers work with continuous measurements, digital computers work with digits (0 and 1) and hybrid computers have both; general-purpose computers do many jobs and special-purpose computers one; and super, mainframe, mini and micro computers differ in size and power, with desktops, laptops, tablets and smartphones as micro computers. The child does not say a smartphone is not a computer. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say how a computer is classified by function, purpose or size
sort named computers into groups
pick the type that fits a described job
find the false step in a learner's reason

misconceptions.error: Thinks data and information are the same.

example.question: A list of marks 45, 62, 38 is data. What is the class average?
example.wrong_answer: Data too, they are the same thing
example.correct_answer: Information, because the data was processed

misconceptions.cause: The words are used as if equal.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Data too, they are the same thing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Data is raw; information is data made useful by processing.
misconceptions.feedback: Data is raw facts. Information is data that has been processed so it means something.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a computer is accurate even when the person types the wrong thing in.

example.question: A clerk types a wrong price. What will the computer print?
example.wrong_answer: The right price, computers never make mistakes
example.correct_answer: The wrong price, from wrong input

misconceptions.cause: Accuracy is mixed up with being right.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The right price, computers never make mistakes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A computer is exact in its sums; it cannot know your typing was wrong.
misconceptions.feedback: A computer is accurate at the working, but wrong input gives wrong output.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks diligence means a computer gets tired and must rest like a person.

example.question: What does diligence mean for a computer?
example.wrong_answer: It gets tired and needs rest
example.correct_answer: It can work for long hours without getting tired

misconceptions.cause: The word is read for people.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It gets tired and needs rest" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A person tires; a computer repeats the same work without losing care.
misconceptions.feedback: Diligence means it works for long hours without tiring or losing care.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a computer thinks and decides by itself.

example.question: How does a computer know what to do?
example.correct_answer: It follows instructions given to it

misconceptions.cause: Films show clever machines.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It thinks for itself" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what a computer does with no program.
misconceptions.feedback: A computer follows the instructions it is given. It does not think for itself.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a computer can do only one kind of job.

example.question: Which characteristic means a computer can do many kinds of jobs?

misconceptions.cause: The child does not know the word.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Diligence" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List what a laptop does: write, draw, play, calculate.
misconceptions.feedback: Versatility is doing many different kinds of jobs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a smartphone is not a computer.

example.question: Is a smartphone a computer?
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is a micro computer

misconceptions.cause: The child links computers with big screens.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only a desktop is" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A phone takes input, processes, stores and gives output.
misconceptions.feedback: A smartphone is a small computer: it takes input, processes, stores and gives output.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the sizes: thinks mini and micro computers are the biggest.

example.question: Which is the biggest and most powerful type?

misconceptions.cause: The names suggest nothing about size order.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Micro computer" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Order them from biggest: super, mainframe, mini, micro.
misconceptions.feedback: The order from biggest is super, mainframe, mini and micro. A laptop is a micro computer.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an analogue computer is just an old computer or not a computer at all.

example.question: What does an analogue computer work with?
example.correct_answer: Continuous measurements such as temperature or speed

misconceptions.cause: The word sounds old.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only old data" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A petrol pump meter reads a flow, not digits alone.
misconceptions.feedback: Analogue computers work with continuous quantities, such as temperature, speed or flow.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks special purpose means weak or low quality.

example.question: A computer in a washing machine does only one job. What type is it?

misconceptions.cause: Special sounds like a poor copy.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A weak general-purpose computer" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: It is built for one job and does it well.
misconceptions.feedback: A special-purpose computer is built for one job. General-purpose computers do many jobs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Say why drawing is used to communicate, and tell artistic drawing from technical drawing
skills.mastery: The child says a drawing shows shape, size and parts that words describe badly and that anyone can read the same plan, and that an artistic drawing shows feeling or beauty while a technical drawing gives exact shape and size by rules so a worker can make the thing. The child does not say technical drawings are for decoration or that artists never measure. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say what a drawing communicates better than words
sort a described drawing as artistic or technical
say who uses technical drawings
find the false step in a learner's reason

skills.name: Name the types of lines in drawing and what each is used for
skills.mastery: The child says the thick continuous line draws the outline and visible edges, the thin continuous line draws dimension lines and projection lines, the dashed line shows hidden detail, and the chain line (long and short dashes) shows the centre of a round part or the line of symmetry. misconceptions.error: Thinks financial goals are only for rich people.

example.question: Who needs financial goals?

misconceptions.cause: Goals sound like big plans.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only rich people" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A child saving for a shoe has a goal.
misconceptions.feedback: Everyone who handles money, even a little, gains from goals.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Treats a goal as a wish.

example.question: What makes a goal different from a wish?
example.correct_answer: A goal has a plan and a date

misconceptions.cause: The two words are used alike.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, they are the same" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A wish says "I want"; a goal says how and when.
misconceptions.feedback: A goal has a plan, an amount and a date. A wish does not.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts wants before needs when setting goals.

example.question: A learner has little money. What comes first?

misconceptions.cause: Wants feel urgent.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A new game" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Needs first, then wants.
misconceptions.feedback: Needs come before wants when money is limited.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Ignores the time available for a goal.

example.question: Which factor says how soon a goal can be reached?

misconceptions.cause: Time is not seen as a factor.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Colour of the notebook" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: More time means smaller savings each week.
misconceptions.feedback: Income, cost and time decide how soon a goal can be reached.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gets the SMART letters wrong.

example.question: What does the A in SMART stand for?

misconceptions.cause: The word is guessed.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Ambitious" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: S, M, A, R, T: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound.
misconceptions.feedback: SMART means Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks "save more money" is a good goal.

example.question: Which is a SMART goal?
example.correct_answer: Save 1,200 shillings in 12 weeks by saving 100 shillings a week

misconceptions.cause: The child does not see what is missing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Save more money" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: how much, how, by when?
misconceptions.feedback: A SMART goal names an amount, a way and a date.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any goal with a number is SMART.

example.question: A learner with 100 shillings a week aims to save 1 million shillings in a month. Is it SMART?

misconceptions.cause: A number seems enough.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it has a number" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Weekly income decides what is realistic.
misconceptions.feedback: A number is not enough. The goal must also be achievable and realistic.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Takes the selling price as the profit.

example.question: A trader buys a bag for 400 shillings and sells it for 500. What is the profit?

misconceptions.cause: The money received feels like gain.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "500 shillings" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Profit is what is left after paying for the goods.
misconceptions.feedback: Profit is selling price minus buying price.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Adds or subtracts instead of dividing to find the weeks needed to save.

example.question: To save 1,200 shillings at 100 shillings a week, how many weeks are needed?

misconceptions.cause: Two numbers are added without thought.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "1,300 weeks" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Count the 100s in 1,200.
misconceptions.feedback: Divide the goal by the amount saved each week.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the profit on one item as the profit on the whole batch.

example.question: A trader earns 10 shillings profit on each of 20 loaves. What is the total profit?

misconceptions.cause: The number of items is forgotten.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "10 shillings" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Multiply the profit on one by the number sold.
misconceptions.feedback: Total profit is profit on one item times the number sold.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Subtracts the selling price from the buying price.

example.question: Buying 60, selling 75. Profit?

misconceptions.cause: The order of subtracting is reversed.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Minus 15 shillings" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Selling price is the bigger number when there is a profit.
misconceptions.feedback: Profit is selling price minus buying price.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
